s92-np-005.text: To ensure a smooth transition from APU generator power to main generator power during engine runup, what is the correct AC generator switching sequence? -- Correct: Turn AC GEN NO. 2 ON, wait at least one second, then turn AC GEN NO. 1 ON. s92-np-010.text: What is the minimum idle time required to cool the engines prior to a normal shutdown? -- Correct: 2 minutes at idle (or below 90% Ng for 2 minutes, including at least 60 seconds at idle, if 2 full minutes at idle is not operationally possible). s92-np-048.text: When changing from APU generator or main generator power to AC external power, what does the RFM require on the AC external power switch? -- Correct: Select RESET before selecting ON. SHUTDOWN NOTE: when transitioning from either APU generator or main generator power to AC external power, select RESET on the AC external power switch prior to selecting ON.
s92-np-048.note: SHUTDOWN p.2-23 NOTE after step 5: transitioning from APU generator or main generator power to AC external power, select RESET on the AC external power switch prior to selecting ON. (DOC 86) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-049.text: For a smoother transition from main generator power to APU generator power at shutdown, what sequence does the RFM give? -- Correct: One DC CONV OFF, AC GEN NO. 1 OFF, wait at least one second, AC GEN NO. 2 OFF, then the DC CONV back ON. To provide a smoother transition from main generator power to APU generator power, turn OFF either main DC converter switch, turn AC GEN NO. 1 OFF, wait at least one second, and then turn AC GEN NO. 2 OFF. Turn the converter ON once both AC generators are off. (Steps: DC CONV 1 or 2 — OFF; AC GEN NO. 1 — OFF; AC GEN NO. 2 — OFF; both DC CONV — ON.)
s92-np-049.note: SHUTDOWN p.2-23 NOTE and steps 7-10: DC CONV 1 or 2 OFF, AC GEN NO. 1 OFF, wait at least one second, AC GEN NO. 2 OFF, both DC CONV ON. (DOC 86) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-050.text: While cooling the engines at idle before shutdown, what is the pilot permitted to do with the throttles? -- Correct: Move them slightly above idle to keep Nr above the lower avoid range. While cooling the engines at idle, the pilot is permitted to move the throttles slightly above idle to maintain Nr above the lower avoid range.
s92-np-050.note: SHUTDOWN p.2-24 NOTE after step 11: while cooling at idle, pilot may move throttles slightly above idle to maintain Nr above the lower avoid range. (DOC 87) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-051.text: In the SHUTDOWN procedure, how often is the FIRE DET test done, and under what condition should the detectors be checked? -- Correct: Once per day, with the engine and APU bays heated to normal operating temperature. SHUTDOWN step 12: FIRE DET — TEST (once per day), using INBD, NORM, OUTB and NORM. NOTE: the engine and APU fire detectors should be checked once a day with the engine and APU bays heated to normal operating temperature.
s92-np-051.note: SHUTDOWN p.2-24 step 12 FIRE DET — TEST (Once per day); NOTE: engine and APU fire detectors checked once a day with engine and APU bays heated to normal operating temperature. (DOC 87) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-052.text: During shutdown, by what Nr should the droop stops be verified in, and what if they do not come in with both throttles at idle? -- Correct: By 50% Nr; if not, shut one engine off to decrease idle Nr, still complying with the required cool down. SHUTDOWN step 13: droop stops — verify in by 50% Nr. NOTE: if the droop stops do not come in with both throttles at idle, shut one engine off to decrease idle Nr. Comply with required engine cool down.
s92-np-052.note: SHUTDOWN p.2-24 step 13 Droop stops — verify in by 50% Nr; NOTE: if not in with both throttles at idle, shut one engine off to decrease idle Nr; comply with required engine cool down. (DOC 87) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-053.text: An engine was shut down without the 2 minute cool down (emergency shutdown). What does the RFM require? -- Correct: Motor it for 1 minute and until TGT is below 150°C, restart within 5 minutes, then run 2 minutes at IDLE. If the engine was not cooled for 2 minutes prior to shutdown (emergency shutdown): motor the engine for 1 minute and until TGT is less than 150°C; start the engine within 5 minutes of engine shutdown; operate the engine for 2 minutes at IDLE; then shut the engine down or continue flight operations.
s92-np-053.note: SHUTDOWN p.2-24 step 14 and p.2-24A a-d: motor for 1 minute and until TGT less than 150°C; start within 5 minutes of shutdown; operate 2 minutes at IDLE; shut down or continue flight operations. (DOC 87, 88) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-054.text: An engine was not properly cooled before shutdown and was not restarted within 5 minutes. When may it be restarted? -- Correct: Not for 4 hours. If the engine was not properly cooled and was not restarted within 5 minutes, do not restart the engine for 4 hours.
s92-np-054.note: SHUTDOWN p.2-24A: if not properly cooled and not restarted within 5 minutes, do not restart the engine for 4 hours. (DOC 88) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-055.text: When may the quick launch procedures be used? -- Correct: Only when no maintenance has been done after the Alert Checklist was completed. The quick launch procedures will only be used when no maintenance has been accomplished after the Alert Checklist is completed. Ensure proper fuel loading for the mission.
s92-np-055.note: QUICK LAUNCH PROCEDURES p.2-25 NOTE: only used when no maintenance has been accomplished after the Alert Checklist is completed; ensure proper fuel loading for the mission. (DOC 89) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-056.text: A helicopter is prepared for a quick launch immediately after shutdown following a flight. Which checklists are considered completed? -- Correct: All required checklists up to the Alert Checklist. Prior to assuming quick launch status, the helicopter is run up to include BEFORE STARTING ENGINES, COCKPIT EQUIPMENT CHECKS, STARTING ENGINES, ROTOR ENGAGEMENT AND ENGINE RUNUP, AFTER LANDING and SHUTDOWN. A helicopter prepared for a quick launch immediately after shutdown, following a flight, is considered to have all required checklists completed up to the Alert Checklist.
s92-np-056.note: QUICK LAUNCH PROCEDURES p.2-25: run-up to include listed checks; a helicopter prepared for quick launch immediately after shutdown following a flight is considered to have all required checklists completed up to the Alert Checklist. (DOC 89) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-057.text: In the ALERT CHECKLIST, how are the generator switches and the fuel selectors set? -- Correct: AC GEN NO. 1 and NO. 2 ON, APU GEN ON, fuel DIRECT. ALERT CHECKLIST: external power — positioned, if required; INT and EXT LIGHTS — as required; PITOT HT and ANTI ICE ENGINE — as required; AIR SRCE HEAT/START — ENG; AC GEN NO. 1 and NO. 2 — ON; APU GEN — ON; NO. 1 and NO. 2 FUEL — DIRECT; rotor brake — as required.
s92-np-057.note: ALERT CHECKLIST p.2-26 steps 1-8: AIR SRCE HEAT/START ENG, AC GEN NO. 1 and NO. 2 ON, APU GEN ON, NO. 1 and NO. 2 FUEL DIRECT. (DOC 90) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-058.text: How does the RFM divide the duties between the Flying Pilot (FP) and the Non-Flying Pilot (NFP) during Category A takeoffs and landings? -- Correct: FP flies on outside references with occasional PFD cross checks; NFP announces decision points and gives verbal guidance on errors. The Category A maneuvers may be flown from either the pilot or copilot seat. They use outside references supplemented by the cockpit instruments. The Flying Pilot should concentrate on outside references with occasional cross checks of the PFD to ensure that performance parameters are met. The Non-Flying Pilot should aid the FP by announcing decision points and providing verbal guidance when errors occur in performance parameters and/or flight path.
s92-np-058.note: TAKEOFF AND LANDING PROCEDURES p.2-29 Pilot duties: either seat; FP concentrates on outside references with occasional PFD cross checks; NFP announces decision points and gives verbal guidance on errors. (DOC 93) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-059.text: During OEI rejected vertical takeoffs and all continued takeoffs, when should the Non-Flying Pilot call out rotor speed? -- Correct: When Nr is outside the desired range, i.e. not between 100 and 104%. Examples of NFP duties: announce when the aircraft attains the TDP or LDP airspeed and/or altitude; during vertical takeoffs, announce when the actual rate of climb deviates significantly from the desired rate; during OEI rejected vertical takeoffs and all continued takeoffs, announce when the actual Nr is outside the desired range for the maneuver (i.e., not between 100 and 104%); during fly-away maneuvers, announce when Vtoss is attained and if airspeed falls below Vtoss; during OEI vertical land back maneuvers, announce when the ground track deviates from the desired track.
s92-np-059.note: TAKEOFF AND LANDING PROCEDURES p.2-29 NFP duty 3: during OEI rejected vertical takeoffs and all continued takeoffs, announce when actual Nr is outside the desired range (not between 100 and 104%). (DOC 93) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-060.text: What does the RFM CAUTION say about the nose wheel just before liftoff? -- Correct: If swiveled about 180° it will not self-center and will jam up if retracted; above 90°, taxi forward slightly to align it. The nose wheel will not self-center after liftoff if it has swiveled about 180° just before liftoff. If retracted in this position, the nose wheel will jam in the up position and normal extension will not be possible. If the nose wheel is swiveled more than 90°, taxi forward slightly to align it with the fuselage.
s92-np-060.note: CATEGORY A HORIZONTAL TAKEOFF p.2-30 CAUTION (repeated for VERTICAL TAKEOFF p.2-30B): nose wheel will not self-center if swiveled about 180° just before liftoff; if retracted it jams up and normal extension is not possible; if swiveled more than 90°, taxi forward slightly to align it. (DOC 94, 96) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-061.text: After a period of heavy or prolonged wheel brake use, how long should the landing gear stay extended before it is retracted? -- Correct: At least 5 minutes. After a period of heavy or prolonged wheel brake use, leave the landing gear extended for a minimum of 5 minutes before retracting.
s92-np-061.note: CATEGORY A HORIZONTAL TAKEOFF p.2-30 NOTE: after heavy or prolonged wheel brake use, leave landing gear extended for a minimum of 5 minutes before retracting. (DOC 94) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-062.text: For the Category A horizontal takeoff, how is Vtoss related to the TDP speed? -- Correct: Vtoss is the TDP speed plus 15 knots. Step 1: refer to Section IV, Figures 4-8 and 4-9 for TDP and Vtoss (TDP + 15 knots) determination. The green airspeed bug is set at the TDP speed.
s92-np-062.note: CATEGORY A HORIZONTAL TAKEOFF p.2-30 step 1: TDP and Vtoss (TDP + 15 knots) from Figures 4-8 and 4-9; step 2 green bug at TDP speed. (DOC 94) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-063.text: In the Category A horizontal takeoff, after noting the stabilized 10 foot hover torque, how is the acceleration to the TDP speed flown? -- Correct: Increase collective to 10% torque above hover and accelerate at a 10 to 15 foot wheel height. Category A horizontal takeoff: establish a 10 foot hover and note the stabilized hover torque; increase collective to achieve 10% torque greater than hover; lower the nose as necessary to result in a 10 to 15 foot wheel height acceleration to the TDP speed; at TDP, rotate nose up to attain a climbing acceleration to Vtoss; after clearing obstacles, continue acceleration to Vy and retract the landing gear.
s92-np-063.note: CATEGORY A HORIZONTAL TAKEOFF p.2-30 steps 3-7: 10 foot hover, note torque; 10% torque greater than hover; 10 to 15 foot wheel height acceleration to TDP speed; at TDP rotate for climbing acceleration to Vtoss; after obstacles accelerate to Vy, gear up. (DOC 94) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-064.text: How must Category A performance be planned for a rolling takeoff? -- Correct: Add the initial ground roll distance to the Figure 4-8 distances, and use no headwind credit. Category A rejected and continued takeoff distances will be longer than those listed in Section IV when a rolling takeoff is accomplished. To ensure Category A performance during a rolling takeoff, the distance required for the initial ground roll should be added to the rejected/continued takeoff distance from Figure 4-8. Headwind credit should not be used during a rolling takeoff.
s92-np-064.note: CATEGORY A ROLLING TAKEOFF p.2-30A NOTE: distances longer than Section IV; add initial ground roll distance to Figure 4-8 distance; headwind credit should not be used. (DOC 95) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-065.text: During a Category A rolling takeoff, what attitude is held at liftoff, and at what height is the aircraft accelerated to Vtdp? -- Correct: Level to slightly nose low; accelerate between 5 and 15 feet. Category A rolling takeoff: initiate forward taxi not to exceed 35 knots; increase collective to lift off the ground while maintaining a level to slightly nose low attitude; accelerate to Vtdp at an altitude between 5 and 15 feet; adjust pitch attitude to climb at Vtoss. The CAUTION warns that excessive aft cyclic movements during takeoff could cause main rotor to airframe contact or tail to ground contact.
s92-np-065.note: CATEGORY A ROLLING TAKEOFF p.2-30A steps 3-6 and CAUTION: taxi not exceeding 35 knots; lift off level to slightly nose low; accelerate to Vtdp between 5 and 15 feet; climb at Vtoss; excessive aft cyclic could cause main rotor to airframe or tail to ground contact. (DOC 95) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-066.text: To prevent tail cone contact with the ground during landing and operations near the ground, what attitude should be avoided? -- Correct: More than 10° nose up. CATEGORY A APPROACH AND LANDING CAUTION: to prevent tail cone contact with the ground during landing and operations near the ground, avoid attitudes of greater than 10° nose-up.
s92-np-066.note: CATEGORY A APPROACH AND LANDING p.2-30A CAUTION: avoid attitudes greater than 10° nose-up to prevent tail cone contact. (DOC 95) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-067.text: What size helipad are the S-92 ground level helipad procedures and performance data based on? -- Correct: A 102 foot square helipad. The ground level helipad procedures and performance data are based on a 102 foot square helipad.
s92-np-067.note: CATEGORY A — GROUND LEVEL HELIPAD p.2-30B: procedures and performance data based on a 102 foot square helipad. (DOC 96) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-068.text: Before a ground level helipad takeoff, what visual cues does the RFM recommend? -- Correct: Two or three cues in front and on the flying pilot's side, several hundred feet from the pad. Prior to takeoff from the helipad, the pilot should identify visual alignment cues to ensure proper lateral and longitudinal position during the climb and possible reject maneuvers. For best results, use two or three cues both in front of and on the flying pilot's side of the aircraft that are several hundred feet from the pad. For night operations, the helipad and alignment cues shall be illuminated.
s92-np-068.note: CATEGORY A — GROUND LEVEL HELIPAD p.2-30B: identify visual alignment cues; two or three cues in front of and on the flying pilot's side, several hundred feet from the pad; at night helipad and cues illuminated. (DOC 96) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-069.text: For vertical takeoffs from a ground level helipad, what do the maximum and minimum TDP from Figure 4-18 represent? -- Correct: Maximum: highest point for a successful land back. Minimum: lowest point for a fly away with 15 feet clearance. Figure 4-18 provides the maximum TDP, minimum TDP and takeoff distance for vertical takeoffs. The maximum TDP is the maximum height for a successful rejected takeoff (vertical land back maneuver). The minimum TDP is the minimum height for a successful continued takeoff (fly away maneuver) providing 15 foot clearance from the takeoff surface.
s92-np-069.note: CATEGORY A VERTICAL TAKEOFF — GROUND LEVEL HELIPAD p.2-30B NOTE: maximum TDP = maximum height for successful rejected takeoff (land back); minimum TDP = minimum height for successful continued takeoff (fly away) with 15 foot clearance. (DOC 96) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-070.text: When conducting a vertical takeoff near obstacles within the takeoff distance of the helipad, how low may the TDP be? -- Correct: No lower than the minimum TDP plus the obstacle height. When conducting takeoffs in the vicinity of obstacles, the TDP should be no lower than the "minimum TDP" plus the obstacle height for obstacles within takeoff distance of the helipad.
s92-np-070.note: CATEGORY A VERTICAL TAKEOFF — GROUND LEVEL HELIPAD p.2-30B NOTE: near obstacles, TDP no lower than minimum TDP plus obstacle height for obstacles within takeoff distance. (DOC 96) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-071.text: In the Category A vertical takeoff from a ground level helipad, how is the vertical climb to the TDP flown? -- Correct: About 20% above HIGE torque, Nr not below 105%, and 850 to 1150 FPM at the TDP. Hover at 10 feet wheel height and note the torque; descend to a wheels light hover; establish a vertical climb with power set approximately 20% above HIGE torque. Do not exceed maximum takeoff power and do not droop the rotor below 105%. Adjust collective to attain between 850 and 1150 FPM rate of climb at the TDP.
s92-np-071.note: CATEGORY A VERTICAL TAKEOFF p.2-30C steps 4-7: 10 ft hover note torque; wheels light hover; vertical climb approximately 20% above HIGE torque, not exceeding maximum takeoff power, not drooping below 105%; 850 to 1150 FPM at the TDP. (DOC 97) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-072.text: In the all engines operating Category A vertical takeoff, what pitch attitudes are used after climbing through the TDP? -- Correct: 5 to 10° below the horizon to accelerate, then about 5° nose up approaching Vtoss. After climbing through the TDP, rotate the aircraft to a pitch attitude of 5 to 10° below the horizon and accelerate toward Vtoss. When approaching Vtoss, rotate to an attitude of approximately 5° nose up and climb at Vtoss or above. After clearing obstacles, accelerate to Vy and retract the landing gear.
s92-np-072.note: CATEGORY A VERTICAL TAKEOFF p.2-30C steps 8-10: after TDP rotate 5 to 10° below the horizon and accelerate toward Vtoss; approaching Vtoss rotate approximately 5° nose up, climb at Vtoss or above; after obstacles Vy, gear up. (DOC 97) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-073.text: What does the minimum LDP for a ground level helipad approach provide, and how is it adjusted for obstacles? -- Correct: A balked landing with 25 feet clearance (15 feet over a 10 foot obstacle); add obstacle height above 10 feet. The minimum LDP is the lowest height from which the aircraft can perform a balked landing with 25 feet of clearance from the landing surface, which provides 15 feet of clearance from a 10 foot obstacle. When obstacles greater than 10 feet high are in the balked landing path, the LDP shall not be lower than the published minimum LDP plus the obstacle height that is in excess of 10 feet.
s92-np-073.note: CATEGORY A GROUND LEVEL HELIPAD APPROACH AND LANDING p.2-30C NOTE: minimum LDP = lowest height for balked landing with 25 feet clearance, giving 15 feet over a 10 foot obstacle; obstacles over 10 feet: LDP not lower than minimum LDP plus obstacle height in excess of 10 feet. (DOC 97) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-074.text: On the Category A ground level helipad approach, what airspeed and descent rate apply until the flare, and what changes in a strong headwind? -- Correct: At or above 35 KIAS and at or below 500 FPM; in high headwinds fly faster to keep at least 20 knots groundspeed. Establish an approach to arrive at the LDP no slower than 35 KIAS, with no more than a 500 FPM rate of descent. In the presence of high head winds, increase approach speed to ensure at least 20 knots of ground speed. Maintain airspeed at or above 35 KIAS and a rate of descent at or below 500 FPM until the flare.
s92-np-074.note: CATEGORY A GROUND LEVEL HELIPAD APPROACH AND LANDING p.2-30C step 3 and NOTE (high head winds: increase approach speed for at least 20 knots ground speed); p.2-30D step 4: at or above 35 KIAS and at or below 500 FPM until the flare. (DOC 97, 98) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-075.text: What are the two FADEC training modes used to practise Category A procedures? -- Correct: Dual engine training, which biases indicated TGT and torque, and training idle, which simulates an engine failure. To allow for the safe practice of Category A procedures, the training mode is used to simulate maximum power dual engine and OEI operation without affecting TBO. Two modes are available: dual engine training, which biases indicated TGT and torque in the precise ratio for the reduced weight training WAT curve, and a training idle mode that simulates an engine failure of the engine selected.
s92-np-075.note: TRAINING MODE p.2-30D: simulates maximum power dual engine and OEI operation without affecting TBO; dual engine training biases indicated TGT and torque for the reduced weight training WAT curve; training idle mode simulates an engine failure of the selected engine. (DOC 98) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-076.text: Before flying in training mode, what must the crew make sure of, and how is training mode exited? -- Correct: The aircraft is loaded within the training WAT curve; exit with the OEI TRAIN switches to DUAL, then OFF. CAUTION: ensure that the aircraft is properly loaded within the training WAT curve prior to commencing flight operations in training mode (see Part 2, Section III). Procedure: OEI TRAIN master switch — TRAIN, note blue TRAIN annunciation on the PFD and EICAS pages; follow Category A takeoff and landing procedures; to practise OEI operation, OEI TRAIN idle switch — #1 or #2 TRNG IDLE and follow the Single Engine Failure procedures; OEI TRAIN switches — DUAL, OFF to exit training mode.
s92-np-076.note: TRAINING MODE p.2-30D CAUTION: properly loaded within the training WAT curve; steps 1-5: OEI TRAIN master switch TRAIN, blue TRAIN annunciation; #1 or #2 TRNG IDLE; OEI TRAIN switches DUAL, OFF to exit. (DOC 98) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-077.text: The rotor was drooped while flying a manoeuvre in training mode. What must be done before exiting training mode? -- Correct: Lower the collective and let Nr recover to 105%. CAUTION: if the rotor has been drooped in the execution of the maneuver, lower the collective and allow rotor speed to recover to 105% before exiting training mode. NOTE: training mode must be exited completely before TRNG IDLE may be selected a second time.
s92-np-077.note: TRAINING MODE p.2-31 CAUTION: rotor drooped, lower collective and allow Nr to recover to 105% before exiting training mode; NOTE: exit completely before TRNG IDLE selected a second time. (DOC 99) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-078.text: What must be done before TRNG IDLE can be selected a second time? -- Correct: Training mode must be exited completely. Training mode must be exited completely before TRNG IDLE may be selected a second time.
s92-np-078.note: TRAINING MODE p.2-31 NOTE: training mode must be exited completely before TRNG IDLE may be selected a second time. (DOC 99) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-079.text: How is the Category B takeoff flown? -- Correct: 10% torque above hover, accelerate at 10 to 15 feet to 45 KIAS, then rotate for a climbing acceleration to 70 KIAS. Category B takeoff: establish a 10 foot hover and note the stabilized hover torque; increase collective to achieve 10% torque greater than hover; lower the nose as necessary to result in a 10 to 15 foot wheel height acceleration to 45 KIAS; at 45 KIAS, rotate nose up to attain a climbing acceleration to 70 KIAS; after clearing obstacles, continue acceleration to Vy and retract the landing gear.
s92-np-079.note: CATEGORY B TAKEOFF p.2-32 steps 1-5: 10 ft hover; 10% torque above hover; 10 to 15 ft wheel height acceleration to 45 KIAS; at 45 KIAS rotate for climbing acceleration to 70 KIAS; after obstacles Vy, gear up. (DOC 100) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-080.text: How are the aircraft and engines set up for the ground power assurance check? -- Correct: Other engine at IDLE, heat and engine anti-ice OFF, nose into wind, 50% Q or more on the checked engine. Ground power assurance: throttle — IDLE (on engine that is not to be checked); COCKPIT and CABIN HEAT — OFF; ANTI-ICE ENGINE NO. 1 and NO. 2 — OFF; MFD — select UTIL → EPAC on one display; heading — nose into wind; collective — adjust to 50% Q or greater (on engine to be checked); INIT bezel key — PRESS.
s92-np-080.note: GROUND POWER ASSURANCE p.2-32A steps 1-7: throttle IDLE on engine not checked; heat OFF; engine anti-ice OFF; UTIL → EPAC; nose into wind; collective 50% Q or greater on engine checked; INIT. (DOC 101) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-081.text: What power margin assures published performance on its own, without looking at the trend? -- Correct: +5° or higher. If power margin is +5° or higher, then published performance is assured. If it is less than +5°, three further conditions must all be true to assure published performance.
s92-np-081.note: GROUND POWER ASSURANCE p.2-32A step 8a and INFLIGHT POWER ASSURANCE p.2-33 step 6a: power margin +5° or higher, published performance assured. (DOC 101, 103) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-082.text: The power margin is less than +5°. Which three conditions must all be true for published performance to be assured? -- Correct: Trended margin +5° or above; this point no more than 12° below the trend; no three consecutive flights below +5°. If power margin is less than +5°, the following three statements must be true to assure published performance: the trended power margin (average of the last ten power assurance checks) must be +5° or above; this single point power margin must be no more than 12° below the trended power margin; no three consecutive flights can have less than +5° power margin.
s92-np-082.note: GROUND POWER ASSURANCE p.2-32A step 8b(1)-(3) and INFLIGHT p.2-33 step 6b: trended margin (average of last ten checks) +5° or above; single point no more than 12° below trend; no three consecutive flights below +5°. (DOC 101, 103) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-083.text: If the power assurance conditions are not met, what does the RFM say for the ground check, and what for the inflight check? -- Correct: Ground: engine maintenance must be done prior to flight. Inflight: published performance is not assured. Ground power assurance: if the conditions of steps a. or b. are not true, engine maintenance must be performed prior to flight. Inflight power assurance: if the conditions of steps a. or b. are not true, published performance is not assured.
s92-np-083.note: GROUND POWER ASSURANCE p.2-32A step 8c: engine maintenance must be performed prior to flight; INFLIGHT POWER ASSURANCE p.2-33 step 6c: published performance is not assured. (DOC 101, 103) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-084.text: During the ground power assurance check, a single point power margin varies from the average margin by more than 12°. What should be done? -- Correct: Repeat the check up to three times, with three minutes at idle to cool down between checks. Should the single point power margin value vary from the average margin by more than 12°, the accuracy of the point should be verified by repeating the check up to three times, allowing three minutes at idle for cool down between checks.
s92-np-084.note: GROUND POWER ASSURANCE p.2-32A NOTE after step 7: single point margin varying from average by more than 12°, verify by repeating the check up to three times, three minutes at idle for cool down between checks. (DOC 101) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-085.text: What flight condition does the inflight power assurance check require, and when is INIT pressed? -- Correct: Level flight stabilized above 80 KIAS; INIT on both engines after 15 seconds at stabilized airspeed. Inflight power assurance: attain level flight at a stabilized airspeed above 80 KIAS; COCKPIT and CABIN HEAT — OFF; ANTI-ICE ENGINE NO. 1 and NO. 2 — OFF (if OAT is above 5°C); MFD — select UTIL → EPAC on one display; INIT bezel key — PRESS (on both engines after 15 seconds at stabilized airspeed).
s92-np-085.note: INFLIGHT POWER ASSURANCE p.2-32A step 1 (level flight, stabilized airspeed above 80 KIAS) and p.2-32B steps 3-5 (engine anti-ice OFF if OAT above 5°C; INIT on both engines after 15 seconds at stabilized airspeed). (DOC 101, 102) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-086.text: What does the RFM CAUTION require before the flotation system test? -- Correct: Clear the area around the nose and tail floats, in case of an inadvertent float deployment. FLOTATION SYSTEM TEST PROCEDURE CAUTION: to avoid possible injury in the event of inadvertent float deployment, clear the area around the nose and tail floats prior to this test.
s92-np-086.note: FLOTATION SYSTEM TEST PROCEDURE p.2-34 CAUTION: to avoid possible injury in the event of inadvertent float deployment, clear the area around the nose and tail floats prior to this test. (DOC 104) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-087.text: During the flotation system test with AUX FLOTATION at ARM, why must the test stop if any L/R indicator is illuminated? -- Correct: It may mean a faulty immersion switch, which with the amber ARM light on may cause immediate float deployment. Continue the test only if the green TEST light is illuminated and neither L/R indicator is illuminated. Illumination of any L/R indicators may be an indication of a faulty immersion switch. With the ARM (amber) light illuminated, a faulty immersion switch may cause immediate float deployment.
s92-np-087.note: FLOTATION SYSTEM TEST PROCEDURE p.2-34 CAUTION after step 3: continue only if green TEST light on and neither L/R indicator; L/R illumination may indicate a faulty immersion switch; with ARM (amber) light illuminated, a faulty immersion switch may cause immediate float deployment. (DOC 104) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-088.text: With normal servicing, down to what temperature can the S-92 operate, and below what temperature must preheat be used? -- Correct: Down to -40°C; preheat below -25°C. With normal servicing, the aircraft can operate at temperatures down to -40°C. Preheat must be used at temperatures below -25°C.
s92-np-088.note: COLD WEATHER PROCEDURES p.2-34B: normal servicing, operate down to -40°C; preheat must be used below -25°C. (DOC 106) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-089.text: The aircraft has been parked at or below -25°C for 4 hours or longer. What must be pre-heated, and how long before operation must pre-heating start? -- Correct: The main rotor head and main rotor flight control servos, starting at least 1 hour before operation. If the aircraft has been parked in ambient temperatures at or below -25°C for 4 hours or longer, the main rotor head and main rotor flight control servos must be pre-heated prior to aircraft operation, using the pre-heat kit. Pre-heat air temperature is set to approximately 130°F, and pre-heating shall be started a minimum of 1 hour before operation to give components time to warm up.
s92-np-089.note: PRE-HEAT p.2-34B: parked at or below -25°C for 4 hours or longer, main rotor head and main rotor flight control servos must be pre-heated; pre-heat air approximately 130°F; started a minimum of 1 hour before operation. (DOC 106) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-090.text: According to the PRE-HEAT CAUTION, what can result from failing to pre-heat when required? -- Correct: Excessive fluid leakage from the main rotor dampers and flight control servos. PRE-HEAT CAUTION: failure to pre-heat may result in excessive fluid leakage from the main rotor dampers and flight control servos.
s92-np-090.note: PRE-HEAT p.2-34B CAUTION: failure to pre-heat may result in excessive fluid leakage from the main rotor dampers and flight control servos. (DOC 106) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-091.text: How must accumulated ice or snow be removed before starting the aircraft? -- Correct: With heated air or an approved de-icing fluid; never by scraping or chipping. Any accumulations of ice or snow must be removed with heated air or an approved de-icing fluid prior to starting the aircraft; failure to do so may result in significant degradation of flying qualities or performance, unwanted structural effects in flight, or foreign object damage if ice is ingested into an engine. Never remove accumulated ice by scraping or chipping. Main rotor blade covers should be used if the aircraft is to remain outside overnight.
s92-np-091.note: COLD WEATHER PRE-FLIGHT CHECK p.2-34B CAUTIONs: remove ice or snow with heated air or approved de-icing fluid before starting; never by scraping or chipping; main rotor blade covers if outside overnight. (DOC 106) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-092.text: For how long must the flight controls be exercised in the cold weather warm-up, depending on temperature? -- Correct: 1 minute between -17°C and -31°C; 2 minutes between -31°C and -40°C. A cold weather warm-up exercise must be accomplished when the aircraft is to be operated at or below -17°C, exercising the collective independently of the rudder pedals. Between -17°C and -31°C, move the flight controls for 1 minute (collective about 1 1/2 inches and each pedal about 3/4 inch, 30 cycles each). Between -31°C and -40°C, move them for 2 minutes (smaller travel in the first minute, larger in the second).
s92-np-092.note: COLD WEATHER CONTROL EXERCISE p.2-35: required at or below -17°C; -17 to -31°C, 1 minute (collective 1 1/2 in, pedals 3/4 in, 30 cycles); -31 to -40°C, 2 minutes (collective 3/4 then 1 1/2 in, pedals 3/8 then 3/4 in). (DOC 107) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-093.text: The LDI test on a cold soaked aircraft shows "TEST INHIBITED". What should the crew do? -- Correct: Continue the cold weather procedures, warm the hydraulics at 50% Nr and repeat the test. If the LDI test is accomplished on a cold soaked aircraft, the result may show "TEST INHIBITED". In this case, continue with all cold weather procedures and warm the hydraulic system at 50% Nr, then repeat the test with a warm hydraulic system. When operating in an extreme cold weather environment, the daily LDI test may be accomplished at the end of a flight when the hydraulic system is at normal operating temperature.
s92-np-093.note: LEAK DETECTION AND ISOLATION (LDI) TEST p.2-35: TEST INHIBITED on cold soaked aircraft, continue cold weather procedures, warm hydraulics at 50% Nr, repeat; extreme cold, daily LDI may be done at end of flight. (DOC 107) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-094.text: During an engine start below -35°C, oil pressure stays at zero after the start is initiated. When must the start be aborted? -- Correct: If oil pressure does not register within 1 minute after start. During starts in extreme cold weather (below -35°C), oil pressure may remain at zero for the first 15 seconds after initiating the start. Abort the start if oil pressure does not register within 1 minute after start.
s92-np-094.note: ENGINE OPERATION p.2-35 item 1: below -35°C oil pressure may remain at zero for the first 15 seconds; abort if it does not register within 1 minute after start. (DOC 107) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-095.text: In an extreme cold start (below -35°C), the engine oil pressure rises past the red line once it registers. What is normal? -- Correct: Up to 225 psi, falling below 100 psi (top of the green) in about 6 minutes. Once oil pressure begins to register on the gauge, it will increase rapidly and exceed the red line. Oil pressure as high as 225 psi is possible and is normal. Oil pressure will begin to decrease shortly after reaching the peak and, depending on the ambient temperature, may take approximately 6 minutes to fall below 100 psi (the top of the green range). When advancing the throttle, use a slower than normal rate to keep the oil pressure within limits.
s92-np-095.note: ENGINE OPERATION p.2-35 items 2-3: oil pressure may exceed red line; as high as 225 psi possible and normal; approximately 6 minutes to fall below 100 psi (top of green); advance throttle slower than normal. (DOC 107) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-096.text: During an extreme cold weather run-up with the rotor brake used, what is normal for the main gearbox and the rotor? -- Correct: MGB oil pressure up to 115 psi, and 3 to 4 minutes before Np/Nr reaches 24%. Particularly when run-up includes use of the rotor brake, main gearbox oil pressure will increase beyond the normal operating range and may reach as high as 115 psi in extremely cold temperatures; this is normal. The engine FADECs prevent engine acceleration if the rotor brake is on (a safety interlock), and engine acceleration is prevented until Np is approximately 24%. During extreme cold weather run-ups, highly viscous transmission oil will restrict main rotor acceleration, resulting in 3 to 4 minutes delay before Np/Nr reaches 24%. Leave the throttle in ground idle until 24% Np/Nr is attained.
s92-np-096.note: MAIN GEARBOX OIL SYSTEM p.2-36: MGB oil pressure as high as 115 psi in extremely cold temperatures is normal; FADEC interlock prevents acceleration until Np approximately 24%; extreme cold 3 to 4 minutes delay before Np/Nr reaches 24%. (DOC 108) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-097.text: During a cold warm-up at low Nr, one or both TR SVO PRES cautions stay on. What does the RFM say? -- Correct: This is acceptable, but all hydraulic pressure cautions must be off by 40% Nr. During warm-up at low Nr, the hydraulic pumps are flow limited. It is possible to have one or both TR SVO PRES cautions remain on until pump speed is sufficient to meet pressure demand. This behavior is acceptable. All hydraulic pressure cautions must be off by 40% Nr.
s92-np-097.note: MAIN GEARBOX OIL SYSTEM p.2-36 NOTE: pumps flow limited at low Nr; one or both TR SVO PRES cautions may remain on; acceptable; all hydraulic pressure cautions must be off by 40% Nr. (DOC 108) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-098.text: After taxiing through snow and flying immediately, what should the pilot do after touchdown? -- Correct: Test that the wheels roll freely; if frozen brakes stop them, hover taxi to parking. After taxiing through snow, the brakes may freeze once the aircraft is brought to a stop. If the aircraft is flown immediately, the brakes may still be frozen upon landing. After touchdown, test that the wheels roll freely before continuing with a normal ground taxi. If the wheels do not roll freely due to frozen brakes, hover taxi to parking.
s92-np-098.note: TAXIING IN SNOW p.2-36: brakes may freeze; if flown immediately may still be frozen on landing; after touchdown test wheels roll freely; if not, hover taxi to parking. (DOC 108) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-099.text: In some icing conditions with RIPS in AUTO, what change in power required may the crew see as the blades accrete ice between heating cycles? -- Correct: A gradual increase of about 10 to 15% torque, returning to about pre-accretion values after the heating cycle. While operating in the AUTO mode in some icing conditions, the aircrew may experience a gradual increase in power required of approximately 10-15% torque as the main and tail rotor blades are allowed to accrete ice during the blade heating element off-cycle. At higher altitude and gross weight combinations the torque change may exceed these values. At the completion of the blade heating cycle, airframe vibration levels and aircraft power requirements should return to the approximate pre-accretion values.
s92-np-099.note: FLIGHT IN ICING CONDITIONS p.2-36: AUTO mode, gradual increase in power required of approximately 10-15% torque during blade heating off-cycle; may exceed at higher altitude/gross weight; returns to approximate pre-accretion values after the heating cycle. (DOC 108) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-100.text: As RIPS heats one set of opposing main rotor blades, for about how long may the crew feel a slight increase in vertical 2/rev vibration? -- Correct: About 5 seconds, while one blade set has shed its ice and the other has not. As the RIPS progresses through a blade heating cycle, the main rotor system sheds ice from one set of opposing blades and then the other. For the short period of time (approximately 5 seconds) when one blade set has shed its ice and the other set has not, the aircrew may experience a slight increase in aircraft vertical 2/main rotor rev vibrations. Because all the tail rotor blades heat at the same time, the aircrew should not normally experience an increase in medium or high frequency airframe vibrations.
s92-np-100.note: FLIGHT IN ICING CONDITIONS p.2-36: main rotor sheds ice from one set of opposing blades then the other; approximately 5 seconds of slight increase in vertical 2/main rotor rev vibrations; all tail rotor blades heat at the same time. (DOC 108) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-101.text: What is the normal RIPS operating mode, and what must be on before entering icing conditions? -- Correct: AUTO; RIPS AUTO or a manual mode, plus engine anti-ice, pitot heat and windshield anti-ice. The normal/recommended operating mode for the RIPS is the AUTO mode. Either the RIPS AUTO mode or a manual mode should be selected prior to flight into icing conditions. The engine anti-ice, pitot heat, and windshield anti-ice should also be on prior to entering icing conditions.
s92-np-101.note: FLIGHT IN ICING CONDITIONS p.2-36: normal/recommended RIPS mode AUTO; AUTO or manual mode selected prior to flight into icing; engine anti-ice, pitot heat and windshield anti-ice on prior to entering icing. (DOC 108) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-102.text: Which signs may indicate that the aircraft has entered freezing drizzle/rain, SLD or other conditions outside the RIPS design envelope? -- Correct: Steadily rising power or vibration, moisture on the windscreen, ice on the overhead windows, erratic or full-scale ice rate meter. Consistently increasing or significant changes in power requirements or airframe vibration levels (i.e. not periodic) could indicate an environment outside the RIPS design envelope (freezing drizzle/rain, supercooled large drops, or conditions outside the certified envelope). Secondary indications include moisture on the windscreen, ice accretion on the cockpit overhead windows, large/erratic fluctuations of the ice rate meter, or a full-scale deflection of the ice rate meter. The aircrew should exit such conditions as soon as possible.
s92-np-102.note: FLIGHT IN ICING CONDITIONS p.2-36/2-37: consistently increasing or non-periodic changes in power or vibration; secondary indications moisture on windscreen, ice on cockpit overhead windows, large/erratic or full-scale ice rate meter; exit as soon as possible. (DOC 108, 109) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-103.text: Why does the RFM CAUTION against hovering low over water with an OAT below +5°C? -- Correct: Recirculated rotor wash can cause icing like freezing drizzle/rain or SLD, outside the RIPS envelope; hover higher. Flight in rotor wash from an over water hover with an OAT less than 5°C could result in an icing condition similar to that experienced in freezing drizzle/rain or SLD and is outside the certified envelope of the RIPS. If the OAT is below +5°C and a hover over water is necessary, hover height should be increased to avoid recirculation.
s92-np-103.note: FLIGHT IN ICING CONDITIONS p.2-37 CAUTION: over water hover rotor wash with OAT below 5°C could give icing like freezing drizzle/rain or SLD, outside RIPS certified envelope; increase hover height to avoid recirculation. (DOC 109) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-104.text: What does the HIGH WIND GROUND PROCEDURES WARNING say about starting or stopping the rotor in strong or gusty winds? -- Correct: The blades may droop below normal; keep all equipment and personnel clear of the rotor arc. HIGH WIND GROUND PROCEDURES WARNING: the rotor blades may droop below normal levels when starting or stopping the rotor in strong and/or gusty winds. Ensure all equipment and personnel are clear of the rotor arc prior to starting or stopping the rotor.
s92-np-104.note: HIGH WIND GROUND PROCEDURES p.2-38 WARNING: rotor blades may droop below normal levels when starting or stopping in strong and/or gusty winds; ensure equipment and personnel clear of the rotor arc. (DOC 110) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-105.text: Above what wind speed is the high wind rotor start procedure recommended, and up to what wind have rotor starts been demonstrated? -- Correct: Recommended above 30 knots; demonstrated up to 55 knots. Rotor starts have been demonstrated in winds up to 55 knots. The high wind rotor start procedure is recommended when starting the aircraft in winds above 30 knots. (Rotor stops have been demonstrated in winds up to 45 knots.)
s92-np-105.note: HIGH WIND ROTOR START PROCEDURE p.2-38: starts demonstrated in winds up to 55 knots; recommended above 30 knots; HIGH WIND ROTOR SHUTDOWN p.2-39 stops demonstrated up to 45 knots. (DOC 110) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-106.text: How are the aircraft and rotor set up before a high wind rotor start? -- Correct: Nose into wind, blades in an X at 45° to the axis, rotor brake at 450 psi or more. High wind rotor start: align the aircraft with the nose into the prevailing wind; position the main rotor blades in an X configuration with the blades 45° from the axis of the aircraft; apply the rotor brake prior to engine start with at least 450 psi of brake pressure; with the ground pump on, position the flight controls (pedals and longitudinal cyclic centered, lateral cyclic 1/2 inch right of center, collective one inch above full down); turn off the ground pump; start both engines against the rotor brake.
s92-np-106.note: HIGH WIND ROTOR START PROCEDURE p.2-38 steps 1-6: nose into prevailing wind; blades in X, 45° from aircraft axis; rotor brake at least 450 psi before engine start; controls set with ground pump on; ground pump off; start both engines against the rotor brake. (DOC 110) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-107.text: In high winds with the rotor stopped, where should the collective be to give minimum static blade flapping? -- Correct: About two to three inches above full down; avoid full down. Avoid positioning the collective full down in high winds with the rotor stopped. Minimum static blade flapping can be achieved with the collective approximately two to three inches above full down. (For the start, the collective is set one inch above full down with the ground pump on; once the ground pump is turned off, the collective will rise above the preset position, which is normal.)
s92-np-107.note: HIGH WIND ROTOR START PROCEDURE p.2-38 NOTEs: avoid collective full down in high winds with rotor stopped; minimum static blade flapping with collective approximately two to three inches above full down; collective rises above preset when ground pump off. (DOC 110) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-108.text: After releasing the rotor brake in a high wind rotor start, how is Nr managed before advancing the throttles to FLY? -- Correct: Hold Nr between 50 and 55%, and do not exceed 55% until stabilized there for at least one minute. After releasing the rotor brake, slowly lower the collective to full down when system 1 and 2 hydraulic pressure are in the green, and adjust the throttles to maintain Nr between 50 and 55%. CAUTION: do not exceed 55% Nr until the rotor has been stabilized in the 50-55% region for at least one minute. Then advance the throttles to FLY.
s92-np-108.note: HIGH WIND ROTOR START PROCEDURE p.2-38 steps 7-9 (release brake; lower collective full down when hydraulics 1 and 2 green; Nr 50 to 55%) and p.2-39 CAUTION and step 10 (do not exceed 55% until stabilized 50-55% for at least one minute; throttles FLY). (DOC 110, 111) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.

s92-np-109.text: In the high wind rotor shutdown procedure, where is the engine cool down done, and when is the rotor brake applied? -- Correct: Cool down with throttles in FLY; rotor brake between 40 and 25% Nr. High wind rotor shutdown (recommended in winds above 30 knots; stops demonstrated up to 45 knots): align the aircraft nose into the prevailing wind; accomplish the required two minute engine cool down with the throttles in FLY; throttles — IDLE; position the cyclic to avoid droop stop pounding (approximately centered); center the pedals; position the collective two inches above full down; throttles — OFF; rotor brake — apply between 40 and 25% Nr.
s92-np-109.note: HIGH WIND ROTOR SHUTDOWN PROCEDURE p.2-39: demonstrated to 45 knots, recommended above 30 knots; two minute cool down with throttles in FLY; throttles IDLE; cyclic approximately centered; pedals centered; collective two inches above full down; throttles OFF; rotor brake between 40 and 25% Nr. (DOC 111) Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-25.
